strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: practical computation of geodesic interpolation and extrapolation on latent manifolds of autoencoders, connecting the latent-space geometry literature (Arvanitidis et al., Shao et al.) with the time-discrete geodesic calculus of Rumpf & Wirth (2015).

The methodological pipeline is coherent and technically sound: the discrete path energy with constraint ζ(z)=0, the augmented Lagrangian scheme with careful discussion of rank-deficient multipliers and inexact constraints (citing established theory), and the discrete exponential map (11) derived from the first saddle point condition are all well-founded and build on proven convergence results (Rumpf & Wirth, Cor. 4.10 and Thm 5.1).

The learned projection Π_σ via the denoising objective (12) is a clean way to obtain an implicit representation of the latent manifold with unknown codimension, with a nice analytic characterization as a Gaussian-weighted barycenter and a quantified defect O(σ²); the parameter study on the toy torus (fig. 9-10) provides some quantitative evidence on dependence on σ, sample size, architecture, and noise.

The experiments span several distinct settings (discrete shells with isometric autoencoder, SVAE on motion capture with a pulled-back SO(3)^m metric, image data with low-bending/low-distortion autoencoder, and Pose-NDF as a distance function), and the appendix gives substantial implementation detail (architectures, σ values, data generation, algorithm 1).

The paper is clearly written, well organized, and honest about limitations (e.g., slight self-intersections remaining due to filter width σ, sensitivity of exponential maps to numerical inaccuracies, and open questions listed in the conclusion).
weaknesses: Evaluation is predominantly qualitative. Apart from the torus projection-error study, the main results (figs. 4-8, 11-13) are visual comparisons against linear interpolation, with no quantitative metrics (e.g., path energy, decoded-path plausibility scores, distance-based errors, or comparison to ground-truth geodesics on the real datasets). Claims such as 'our geodesics avoid self-intersections more effectively' or 'yields realistic decoded paths' are supported only by pictures.

There is no comparison against the most relevant competing methods, e.g., Sun et al. (2025), which also learns an implicit representation of the latent manifold, or geodesics computed via decoder pullback metrics (Arvanitidis et al.). The related-work discussion asserts differences in approach but the experiments do not demonstrate superiority or even parity on any shared benchmark.

A key practical requirement is underexplored: the pullback metric W_M requires exact/fast Riemannian distances in the data space (e.g., dist_SO(3)^m or shell distances), and the Euclidean metric requires near-isometric encoders. The conclusion acknowledges this, but it substantially limits applicability to general autoencoders (e.g., standard VAEs on natural images), and the paper does not quantify how much accuracy degrades when these assumptions are only approximately met.

Sensitivity to the choice of σ is acknowledged ('suitable values of σ depend on the sampling') but the heuristic for choosing σ in practice is informal; a sensitivity analysis on the real experiments, not just the torus toy model, would strengthen the evidence.

Novelty is moderate: the discrete geodesic calculus and augmented Lagrangian machinery are adapted from Rumpf & Wirth (2015) and Nocedal & Wright, and the projection-from-denoising idea is taken from Alain & Benggio (2014); the contribution is the combination and application to latent manifolds, which is useful but not a fundamentally new method.

No statement about releasing code or data is given, which limits reproducibility despite the detailed appendix (e.g., autoencoder training specifics such as loss weights for the isometric autoencoder are partially deferred to prior work).

strengths: The paper is technically careful: the time-discrete variational geodesic calculus is properly adapted to implicit submanifolds via an augmented Lagrangian with inexact constraints, and the choice of W for different metrics (Euclidean, pullback, data-space distance, KL) is well motivated in A.1.

The idea of learning an approximate projection Πσ via a denoising objective (building on Alain & Bengio, 2014) is a sensible and clean way to obtain an implicit representation of unknown codimension, and the O(σ²)/O(σ) defect discussion adds useful insight.

The experimental scope is reasonably broad, spanning discrete shells (SCAPE), motion capture with an SVAE, image data with a near-isometric autoencoder, and an extension to a third-party distance representation (Pose-NDF), showing the framework is not tied to one autoencoder type.

Appendices provide substantial implementation detail (algorithm for the augmented Lagrangian, architectures, σ choices, data generation), which supports reproducibility of the methodology, and the toy torus parameter study (fig. 10) is a useful sanity check.

The paper is honest about limitations: exponential-map drift (fig. 3), residual self-intersections due to σ, and the fact that efficiency requires near-isometric embeddings or fast data-space distances are all acknowledged.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely a combination of established components: the discrete geodesic calculus is taken from Rumpf & Wirth (2015) including its convergence guarantees, and the implicit representation is a direct application of denoising-autoencoder projections. The genuinely new theory (e.g., convergence of the augmented Lagrangian scheme for inexact constraints ζσ) is missing; the paper only asserts 'we observe that the augmented Lagrangian method works for an inexact implicit function' without analysis.

The evaluation is almost entirely qualitative. There are no quantitative metrics (path energy, constraint violation, geodesic error vs. ground truth, reconstruction quality along paths, or downstream task scores) on the real experiments, so the central claim that geodesics on the latent manifold are meaningfully better than simpler alternatives rests on visual inspection of figures.

Baselines are weak. The main comparison is against linear interpolation in latent space, which is known to be poor. No quantitative comparison against existing geometric approaches (e.g., Chen et al. 2018 metric modification, Arvanitidis et al. 2021/2022 pullback metrics, Sun et al. 2025 implicit-representation metric learning) is provided, even though these are the closest related works.

Efficiency claims are unsubstantiated. No runtimes are reported anywhere, and in the flagship discrete-shells experiment the training data itself must be generated by a 'computationally demanding' classical Riemannian construction (PGA, discrete logarithms/exponentials), which undercuts the motivation of avoiding expensive data-space computations.

Hyperparameter sensitivity on real data is not addressed: σ is chosen manually per experiment ('in our experiments below, we could choose the same σ for similar point cloud densities'), and the systematic study is confined to a toy torus. Guidance for practical use on real latent spaces with unknown sampling density and noise remains anecdotal.
There is no explicit code release or reproducibility statement, and given that the contribution is algorithmic and empirical, others cannot reliably build on or verify the results without it.

The key results depend on favorable structure: the Euclidean metric is used on the latent manifold only because the autoencoder is (near-)isometric, a property most practical autoencoders do not enjoy, and the paper concedes this in the conclusion. Thus the demonstrated applicability to generic latent spaces is narrower than the framing suggests.

Experiments are small-scale (latent dimensions 10–24, single subject/scene per experiment), and the exponential-map section shows accuracy degrading exponentially, offering no mitigation beyond citing known behavior.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: equipping autoencoder latent spaces with a practically usable Riemannian structure is an open and relevant challenge, and the paper clearly articulates its position relative to pullback-metric approaches (Shao et al. 2018; Chen et al. 2018; Arvanitidis et al.) and implicit-representation work (Sun et al. 2025).

The methodology is technically well-grounded: the time-discrete geodesic calculus builds on the proven framework of Rumpf & Wirth (2015) with known convergence guarantees for the discrete path energy and the discrete exponential map, and the augmented Lagrangian treatment of inexact (learned) constraints ζ_σ is a sensible and nontrivial adaptation.

The denoising-based learning of an approximate projection Π_σ (eq. 12) is elegant: it handles arbitrary dimension and codimension, yields an explicit formula as a Gaussian-weighted barycenter, comes with an O(σ²)/O(σ) defect analysis, and is independent of the underlying autoencoder. The parameter study in A.3 (figs. 9-10) systematically supports its empirical properties.

The evaluation spans a diverse set of settings (discrete shells with a shell metric, SVAE on motion capture with a pulled-back SO(3)^m distance, a near-isometric image autoencoder, and an external distance-function representation via Pose-NDF), demonstrating modularity across metrics and autoencoder types, including use of third-party pretrained models.

The paper is clearly written, the mathematical setup (Sections 2-4) is precise, algorithmic details are sufficiently complete for reproducibility (Algorithm 1, architectures, hyperparameters, σ choices), and limitations (dependence on isometry or fast data-space distances, σ sensitivity, residual self-intersections) are discussed honestly in Section 6.
weaknesses: The evaluation is almost entirely qualitative. On the real-data experiments (SCAPE, motion capture, cow images, Pose-NDF) results are shown as decoded sequences judged visually; no quantitative metrics (e.g., path energy, deviation from the manifold, distance distortion vs. ground truth, self-intersection counts) are reported, making the central claim that the method 'yields realistic geodesic paths' hard to verify objectively.

Baselines are very weak: comparisons are essentially against linear interpolation in latent space. No comparison is made against established alternatives for latent-space geodesics, e.g., geodesics under pulled-back decoder metrics (Chen et al. 2018; Arvanitidis et al. 2018) or Sun et al. (2025), so the practical benefit over prior latent-geometry methods remains unquantified.

Only the torus toy example (figs. 2-3) uses a ground-truth implicit representation; even there the comparison against ground truth is visual rather than numeric, and the well-known sensitivity of exponential-map extrapolation to errors in ζ_σ is acknowledged (fig. 3) but not analyzed or quantified.

Originality is moderate: the discrete geodesic calculus is directly inherited from Rumpf & Wirth (2015), and the projection learning is a direct application of Alain & Bengio (2014) to latent point clouds; the main novelty lies in the combination and in the inexact-constraint augmented Lagrangian treatment rather than in new theory.

Practicality of the claimed efficiency gain is not evidenced: no runtimes, memory costs, or comparisons to direct computations on the data-space manifold (which the paper motivates as expensive) are reported, so the reduced-order benefit is asserted but not demonstrated.

No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned, despite the pipeline involving multiple learned components (autoencoders, Π_σ networks) and several tunable choices (σ, K, tolerances) whose sensitivity is only partially characterized on the toy example.

The treatment of nondeterministic encoders/decoders (Section 5.2) explicitly ignores the stochastic nature of the SVAE with only a brief acknowledgment that a KL-based alternative exists (eq. 14); this limits the claimed applicability to VAE-type generative models and to future 'latent distributions' ambitions.

strengths: The paper is mathematically well-grounded: it adapts the time-discrete geodesic calculus of Rumpf & Wirth (2015), which comes with established convergence guarantees for perfect implicit representations, to the practically relevant case of imperfect, learned implicit representations of autoencoder latent manifolds.

The idea of learning an approximate projection via a denoising objective (eq. 13) is simple, principled, and well-characterized: the authors derive the minimizer as a Gaussian-weighted barycenter and quantify the projection defect (O(σ²) in the relative interior, O(σ) near the boundary).

The augmented Lagrangian formulation is thoughtfully adapted to handle inexact constraints ζσ, and the discussion of why the method tolerates a learned (non-vanishing) implicit function is convincing; the discrete exponential map is carefully derived to reproduce the variational geodesics.

The evaluation is broad, covering four quite different settings: isometric autoencoders on discrete shells (SCAPE), spherical VAEs on motion capture with a pulled-back SO(3)^m metric, a near-isometric image autoencoder, and a pure neural distance function (Pose-NDF), demonstrating flexibility with respect to both autoencoder type and metric choice.

Appendix C contains substantive comparisons: quantitative timing and path-energy comparisons against the Stochman library (C.1), a discussion of grid-based and graph-based alternatives (C.2), and empirical comparisons against uncertainty-regularized VAE geodesics (C.3) and the LAND density-based model (C.4), including toy models where projection accuracy is measured against ground truth.
Good parameter studies (figs. 10-11) showing how projection error behaves with sample size, network size, noise level, and σ.

Honest treatment of limitations: the authors acknowledge the remaining self-intersections from finite σ, the need for either fast data-space distances or near-isometric embeddings, and the heuristic choice of σ.
weaknesses: The evaluation is predominantly qualitative. Beyond timing and path energies in Appendix C, there are essentially no quantitative metrics on the real-data experiments (e.g., distance to the data manifold along decoded paths, self-intersection counts, reconstruction quality, or user-visible error measures), making it hard to assess how much better the method is than baselines.

The key claims of robustness to imperfect implicit representations are supported only empirically; no theoretical analysis (even heuristic error bounds relating projection accuracy to geodesic accuracy) is provided for the inexact-constraint case, which is the paper's central novelty over Rumpf & Wirth (2015).

The discrete shells experiment has a circularity concern: the claimed advantage that geodesics 'avoid self-intersections more effectively than linear interpolation' is partly baked in by discarding self-intersecting shapes during training data generation, so the comparison conflates the method with the data curation.

Some baseline comparisons are potentially unfair: in C.3 the Arvanitidis et al. (2022) method is reported to fail to converge, but little detail is given on tuning efforts for the baselines, and the comparison is on a single toy example.

No code release or reproducibility statement is apparent in the manuscript, despite many implementation-sensitive choices (augmented Lagrangian parameters, initial path construction, σ per experiment, network architectures).

The choice of σ is heuristic and problem-dependent ('in our experiments below, we could choose the same σ for similar point cloud densities'), and the paper itself lists the σ-accuracy trade-off as an open question; this limits turn-key applicability.

Single endpoint pairs (or a handful) are shown per experiment with no repetition or statistical treatment, so the stability and typical behavior of the computed geodesics and exponential maps on real data remain unclear.

The practical speed advantage is modest: projection learning takes ~12 minutes and geodesics seconds to minutes, comparable to or slower than some baselines in low dimensions; the efficiency claim rests on low latent dimensionality, which is not stress-tested beyond l=84 (Pose-NDF) without timing details.

strengths: The methodology is mathematically well-grounded: the time-discrete variational geodesic calculus builds on the established convergence theory of Rumpf & Wirth (2015), and the paper carefully cites the conditions (smooth manifold, Lipschitz metric, O(dist^3) approximation of squared distance) under which their discrete schemes are justified.

The idea of representing latent manifolds implicitly via a learned denoising projection Πσ (Section 4) is clean, is independent of the underlying autoencoder, and the derivation of the projection as a Gaussian-weighted barycenter with an O(σ^2) defect analysis is a nice theoretical touch.

The augmented Lagrangian scheme (Section 3) is thoughtfully adapted to inexact constraints ζσ, and the design of the discrete exponential map (functional (12)) avoids second-order differentiation of the projection and decoder networks — a practically relevant detail.

The evaluation spans a genuinely diverse set of settings: isometric autoencoders on discrete shells, spherical VAEs on motion capture, a low-bending/low-distortion autoencoder on images, and even a third-party distance function (Pose-NDF), demonstrating generality of the framework.

Appendix C contains substantive comparisons (Stochman, uncertainty-regularized VAE decoders of Arvanitidis et al., LAND density-based metrics), including timing measurements and discussion of conceptual differences, and Appendix A/B provide reproducibility-oriented details (architectures, σ values, optimizer settings, tolerances).

Limitations and open questions are discussed honestly in the conclusion (dependence of accuracy on sampling density and σ, need for near-isometric embeddings or fast data-space distances, robustness of augmented Lagrangians for inexact constraints).
weaknesses: Evaluation is almost entirely qualitative. The central empirical claims — that computed paths 'adhere to the latent sample distribution', avoid artifacts, and are 'robust' — are supported only by visual inspection of decoded interpolations (Figs. 2, 5-9, 12-14). No quantitative metrics (e.g., path energies vs. baselines, distance-to-manifold of decoded paths, reconstruction fidelity, failure rates across random endpoint pairs) are reported for the real-data experiments.

Robustness of the method to imperfect implicit representations is the headline claim, but it is validated mainly on a single toy torus example (Figs. 3, 10, 11); the real-data experiments never quantify how much the learned projection's inaccuracy degrades the resulting geodesics.

Several comparisons in Appendix C appear anecdotal and potentially favorably configured: e.g., the claim that the Arvanitidis et al. (2022) baseline 'leaves the data manifold and does not converge' rests on one toy example, and hyperparameter choices for baselines vs. the proposed method are not equally tuned.

The flagship discrete-shells experiment (Section 5.1) is somewhat circular: it requires an expensive classical Riemannian construction (PGA with discrete geodesic computations on meshes) to synthesize training data for the autoencoder, which limits the claimed practicality of the approach as a reduced-order tool for shape spaces.

Computational costs are non-trivial and unevenly reported: projection training takes ~10-12 minutes even on toy/low-dimensional examples, individual geodesics take up to several minutes, yet there is no systematic runtime analysis or scaling study with latent dimension or point-cloud size.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, which, combined with many problem-specific hyperparameters (σ, penalty schedules, tolerances η*, µ0, µmax, architectures), hampers reproducibility.

The contribution is incremental in a technical sense: the discrete geodesic calculus is taken from prior work and the projection is a direct application of the Alain & Bengio (2014) denoising estimator; the novelty lies mainly in their combination and the augmented-Lagrangian treatment of inexact constraints, which some reviewers may consider narrow for the main track.

The relationship between the choice of W (Euclidean, pullback, KL) and correctness of the resulting geometry is only informally justified in practice; e.g., in the SVAE experiment the deterministic-mean shortcut and the choice of W_M are made 'for simplicity' without quantifying the resulting approximation error.

strengths: Technically solid and well-grounded framework: the paper adapts the variational time-discrete geodesic calculus of Rumpf & Wirth (2015), which carries existing convergence guarantees for vanishing time steps, to implicitly defined latent manifolds, and carefully addresses the practically important issue of inexact implicit representations (ζ replaced by a learned ζσ = id − Πσ) within an augmented Lagrangian scheme.

The learned projection via the denoising objective (Eq. 13) is a clean, autoencoder-agnostic way to obtain an implicit representation of unknown codimension, and the paper derives its analytic form as a Gaussian-weighted barycenter and quantifies its defect (O(σ²) in the interior, O(σ) near the boundary).

The discrete exponential map scheme (Eqs. 7-12) is a sensible variational counterpart that reproduces discrete variational geodesics, and the authors note a useful computational simplification (no second derivatives of the ζ network required).

Unusually thorough experimental breadth for this type of work: discrete shells with an isometric autoencoder (SCAPE), an SVAE on motion capture data with a pulled-back spherical metric, a near-isometric image autoencoder, and a distance-function-based extension to Pose-NDF, covering Euclidean, pullback, and KL-based metrics.

Appendix C provides substantive comparisons rather than token baselines: against the Stochman parametric pipeline (with timings and path-energy comparison on a torus), against uncertainty-regularized variational decoders (Arvanitidis et al. 2018, 2022), and against density-based metrics (LAND), with honest discussion of trade-offs on both sides.

Reproducibility-relevant details are largely present: architectures, optimizers, σ values, penalty parameters, timings, and data construction pipelines (Sections A.2, A.3, B.1-B.4), plus a parameter study (Fig. 11) on projection accuracy versus point-cloud size, network size, and noise.

The limitations are discussed candidly, e.g., that efficiency requires either fast distance evaluation on M or a (near-)isometric embedding, that slight self-intersections may persist due to finite σ, and that accuracy dependence on sampling density and σ remains open.
weaknesses: Evaluation of the central claims is predominantly qualitative. The claims that geodesics 'follow the data support' and yield 'realistic' interpolations/extrapolations are supported almost entirely by visual inspection of decoded sequences (Figs. 2, 5-9, 12-14). There is no quantitative metric on real-data experiments (e.g., path energy vs. baselines, manifold adherence scores, distance distortion, or downstream task measures), which weakens the empirical evidence for the core contribution.

Quantitative comparisons to baselines are confined to toy settings (torus geodesics vs. Stochman, half-circle vs. LAND, a toy VAE distribution vs. Arvanitidis et al.). On the actual motivating applications (SCAPE, motion capture, images, Pose-NDF), no competing method is run, so the practical superiority over, e.g., pullback-metric geodesics without manifold constraints (shown only once, in Fig. 13 blue) is not systematically established.

Moderate originality: both main ingredients are adaptations of known components — the discrete geodesic calculus and exponential map scheme is taken from Rumpf & Wirth (2015) including its convergence theory, and the learned projection is the classical denoising-autoencoder variational construction of Alain & Bengio (2014). The novelty lies in the combination and in the treatment of inexact constraints, which is valuable but incremental.

The learned projection quality is only validated against ground truth on the synthetic torus. On real latent manifolds, there is no measurement of how projection error (in |ζσ| or normal-direction accuracy) propagates into geodesic error, although this is acknowledged as a key open question in the conclusion.

The method's applicability hinges on restrictive conditions that limit generality: efficiency requires either a known/cheaply computable metric on M or a near-isometric encoder, and the W_M choice needs explicit data-space distances; these requirements exclude the common setting of generic, non-isometric autoencoders, which is exactly where a latent-geometry method would be most useful.

No explicit statement of code release is given; given the many hyperparameters (σ, penalty schedule, tolerances η*, initialization path, K) and problem-dependent rule-of-thumb choices, reproducibility without code would be difficult.

Some claims of robustness of the augmented Lagrangian approach for inexact constraints are asserted ('we observe that the augmented Lagrangian method works... as long as (ζσ, Dζσ) approximate (ζ, Dζ) sufficiently well') without formal characterization or systematic ablation; the conditions under which the method fails are not explored.
